product.title: Understand Git DrillDown in a few minutes
product.description: Git DrillDown is a desktop application for exploring a Git project and performing common Git work without losing sight of the repository, branch or submodule affected by an action.
product.plainDefinition: Think of it as a visual control panel over Git: the application shows the project, asks the native engine to perform an operation, then refreshes the screen with the result.
product.localFirstNote: Most work happens on this computer. A server is contacted only for operations such as fetch, pull, push or Pull Request status.

mentalModel.title: Every action follows the same route
mentalModel.description: The details vary, but the application uses this five-step loop for repository work.

steps.title: You choose an action
steps.plain: For example: open a folder, stage a file or inspect history.

steps.title: The context is identified
steps.plain: The app determines the exact repository, submodule, path and branch involved.

steps.title: The native engine checks and runs it
steps.plain: Rust applies the operation, including locks, caches and safety rules.

steps.title: Git or the filesystem changes
steps.plain: The result is usually local; network tools are used only when the action needs a server.

steps.title: The screen confirms the result
steps.plain: The interface refreshes the relevant status, list, check mark or message.

exampleJourney.title: Concrete example: stage a new file
exampleJourney.description: Staging chooses what will enter the next commit; it does not send anything to a server.

steps.label: 1. Select the file
steps.detail: The Working tree shows a file that Git has not tracked before.

steps.label: 2. Press Stage
steps.detail: The application sends the selected path together with its repository context.

steps.label: 3. Update the Git index
steps.detail: The backend normalizes the path, respects submodule boundaries and stages the file locally.

steps.label: 4. Refresh status
steps.detail: The file moves to the staged state and becomes eligible for the next commit.

system.name: Git DrillDown
system.summary: A Tauri 2 desktop Git client with a dependency-free WebView UI, a Rust/libgit2 backend, selected system Git/gh integrations, and engineering-workflow helpers.
architecturalStyle: Desktop client with WebView presentation and native Rust backend
Layered in deployment, but predominantly two monolithic implementation modules

entities.name: Git DrillDown
entities.summary: The complete desktop application and its build/documentation artifacts.

reasons: Most product behavior is concentrated in two source files
UI and native operations are joined through a broad stringly-typed command surface

entities.name: WebView presentation
entities.summary: Static HTML/CSS and plain JavaScript executed in the Tauri WebView.

reasons: The controller owns most UI state and product workflows
No framework or module loader creates enforcement boundaries

entities.name: Document shell
entities.summary: Declares the complete screen, panels and dialogs loaded by Tauri.

reasons: All screens and dialogs share one document
Structure is static and easy to deploy but grows with every feature

entities.name: Application controller
entities.summary: The effective frontend orchestrator: it owns global state, event wiring, rendering, command dispatch and most workflows.

execution.asyncBehavior: Starts Promise-based IPC calls; render and event handlers stay on the WebView event loop.
execution.parallelism: Overlapping promises are possible, but JavaScript callbacks execute serially.

reasons: 4,300 lines and approximately 185 functions
Presentation, application orchestration and adapter decisions are mixed
Most product flows read and mutate one global state object
Broad incoming dependency from nearly every user action

entities.name: Pure graph model
entities.summary: Pure commit-DAG and ref-selection logic shared by the UI and Node tests.

reasons: Cohesive pure computations
No DOM, IPC or shared mutable application state
Direct automated tests

entities.name: Visual system
entities.summary: Single stylesheet for application layout, themes, component states and responsive behavior.

reasons: One global cascade covers every feature
Visual consistency is centralized but selector ownership is implicit

entities.name: Tauri command boundary
entities.summary: Composition root and serialized command interface between JavaScript and Rust.

reasons: Composition is thin and explicit
The public command surface is large and manually string-matched by JavaScript

entities.name: Native backend
entities.summary: Rust command implementations, Git/filesystem orchestration, caches, locks and provider integrations.

reasons: Nearly all backend responsibilities live in one Rust module
Infrastructure, adapters, DTOs, application services and tests share one compilation unit

entities.name: Repository backend monolith
entities.summary: The effective backend orchestrator and implementation home for every registered command.

reasons: 10,078 lines with multiple unrelated architectural roles
All 79 Tauri commands couple to one module
Change impact and review surface are unusually broad
Integration tests and production implementation are interleaved

entities.name: Diagnostics and build identity
entities.summary: Privacy-conscious performance logging plus embedded source revision identity.

reasons: Focused cross-cutting utility
Avoids logging paths, credentials and command text

entities.name: Cache and lock runtime
entities.summary: Process-global TTL caches and per-path synchronization maps used across Git operations.

reasons: Cache ownership and invalidation are distributed across commands
Several cache keys use caller path strings while write locks canonicalize paths
Maps have no session cleanup policy

entities.name: External process runner
entities.summary: Configures, launches, waits for and force-terminates Git, gh and shell child processes.

execution.parallelism: Each call spawns a child plus a native waiter thread; distinct calls can overlap unless a repository lock serializes them.
execution.cancellation: No cooperative user cancellation. Timeout kills the process after 600 seconds.

reasons: External processes can remain active for up to ten minutes
Waiter threads and force-kill behavior are hand-built
Arbitrary shell execution is intentionally supported by the Terminal

entities.name: Repository loading and status
entities.summary: Builds fast/full repository snapshots, commit windows, branch lists and working-tree status.

execution.blockingWork: libgit2 repository and filesystem scans execute inside spawn_blocking.

reasons: Full status is naturally expensive on very large worktrees
Fast/full load paths duplicate snapshot construction concepts
Correctness depends on cache freshness and explicit invalidation

entities.name: History and graph data
entities.summary: Walks commits and refs and exposes pages, tag details, divergence and path history.

reasons: Backend data construction is coherent
Some potentially large history operations remain synchronous Tauri commands

entities.name: Working tree and commit
entities.summary: Stages, unstages, commits, restores and removes paths while respecting submodule boundaries.

reasons: Mutation correctness crosses parent/submodule repositories
Several mutation commands remain synchronous at the IPC boundary
Manual cache invalidation accompanies mutations

entities.name: Branch and merge workflows
entities.summary: Branch lifecycle, upstream context, merges and conflict resolution.

reasons: All exposed commands are synchronous despite repository traversal and mutation
Conflict workflow state is divided between Git metadata and frontend global state

entities.name: Remote synchronization
entities.summary: Lists remotes and executes fetch, pull, push and publish operations.

reasons: Network child processes are long-running and some endpoints remain synchronous
Command timeout is a backstop, not interactive cancellation

entities.name: GitHub Pull Request adapter
entities.summary: Parses GitHub and GitHub Enterprise remotes, resolves branch/upstream/fork context and queries PR state using gh.

execution.parallelism: A scoped native-thread fan-out queries outgoing and incoming PR candidates concurrently; candidate bases are capped at four.
execution.cancellation: Generation checks skip superseded work before gh dispatch. Already running gh processes continue; frontend ignores stale results.

reasons: Provider parsing, query planning, process execution and presentation DTO mapping share the backend monolith
Correctness depends on remote/upstream/fork topology and external gh authentication

entities.name: Submodule workflows
entities.summary: Resolves exact submodule repositories and implements navigation, version, URL, commit and remote workflows.

reasons: Coordinates two repositories and their separate locks/caches
Some read operations can scan a nested worktree synchronously
Lock ordering safety is maintained by convention and explicit guard drops

entities.name: Compare (future Workbench seed)
entities.summary: Backend tree/content comparison and restore operations for the current synchronized local↔remote path.

execution.algorithm: Frontend line alignment uses O(n×m) LCS with a two-million-cell fallback.

reasons: Conceptually cohesive but split across both monoliths
One global path and remote ref encode a synchronized two-pane assumption
Remote restore performs fetch and file mutation through a synchronous endpoint

entities.name: Stash workflows
entities.summary: Whole-tree and path-scoped stash creation, inspection, restoration and conflict recovery.

reasons: Every command is synchronous and mutates repository/worktree state
Selective restore is operationally complex and coupled to frontend dialogs

entities.name: Engineering workflow integrations
entities.summary: Company-specific Polarion URL validation and Windows-only UTRUD launch behavior.

reasons: Company-specific URLs and tool paths are compiled into generic UI/backend modules
No provider interface or configuration seam isolates these integrations

entities.name: Native and local services
entities.summary: Libraries, filesystem and executables used by the Rust backend.

reasons: Dependencies are few and explicit
Behavior varies by platform and installed tools

entities.name: Embedded libgit2
entities.summary: Primary local Git implementation through the git2 crate with vendored libgit2/OpenSSL.

reasons: Keeps most local Git operations self-contained
Repository handles and filesystem changes still require explicit synchronization

entities.name: System Git CLI
entities.summary: External Git used primarily for network operations and advanced workflows requiring existing user credentials.

reasons: Uses the user's proven Git credential setup
Availability and behavior depend on machine PATH/configuration

entities.name: Filesystem
entities.summary: Direct Rust filesystem traversal, metadata, reading, writing and path deletion.

reasons: Large worktrees make traversal latency platform-sensitive
Filesystem state may change externally between cached observations

entities.name: Remote engineering services
entities.summary: Optional services reached through Git transports, gh or validated browser links.

reasons: The core can operate locally without most services
Network/auth/provider variability affects remote features

entities.name: Git remote servers
entities.summary: Any Git-compatible remote configured in a repository.

reasons: Generic transport boundary through system Git

entities.name: GitHub / GitHub Enterprise
entities.summary: PR provider queried by gh with explicit hostname and owner/repository slug.

reasons: Supported deliberately for public and enterprise hosts
Depends on gh installation and per-host authentication

entities.name: Polarion
entities.summary: Company work-item links inferred from commit-message tokens.

reasons: Host and URL shape are hard-coded in generic source files

entities.name: UTRUD
entities.summary: Windows-only external test-results tool launched for selected r folders.

reasons: Fixed Windows installation path and folder convention
Process is fire-and-forget and outside application lifecycle

entities.name: Build and delivery
entities.summary: Tauri build configuration, platform launchers and Windows packaging workflow.

reasons: Windows automation exists and embeds build identity
macOS launcher consumes an existing bundle rather than defining a repeatable build pipeline
Bundled executable is versioned separately from source edits

entities.name: Automated tests
entities.summary: Pure graph-model Node tests plus extensive Rust tests embedded in repository.rs.

reasons: Backend behavior has broad regression coverage
The 4,300-line UI orchestrator lacks direct integration or browser tests

interfaces.name: Tauri command API
interfaces.protocol: window.__TAURI__.core.invoke(command, camelCase arguments) → Promise of Serde JSON or rejected string error
interfaces.assessment: Explicit and inspectable, but broad, manually named and without generated client contracts. Sync entries call inline in Tauri's generated blocking wrapper.

interfaces.name: Embedded Git interface
interfaces.assessment: Primary local Git boundary; avoids depending on an installed Git executable for routine browsing and mutation.

interfaces.name: System Git interface
interfaces.protocol: git -C <repository> with literal argv, captured stdout/stderr, prompts disabled and timeout
interfaces.assessment: Pragmatic credential reuse, but process lifetime/progress/cancellation are only coarsely modeled.

interfaces.name: GitHub PR interface
interfaces.assessment: Understands enterprise hosts and fork/upstream topology, but is not expressed as a reusable provider trait.

state.name: Application UI state
state.readersWriters: Most rendering and event-handler functions in app.js
state.synchronization: JavaScript event-loop serialization plus scattered request-generation guards
state.risk: A late async result or context confusion can overwrite state for a newer repository/submodule unless each path uses the correct guard.

state.name: Compare/Commander state
state.synchronization: One shared relative path keeps local and remote views aligned.
state.risk: The model does not yet represent two independent pane locations required for Local↔Local Workbench.

state.name: Frontend directory cache
state.synchronization: Explicit cache clears and navigation request generations
state.risk: Correctness depends on invalidation when backend or external filesystem changes occur.

state.name: Backend Git caches
state.synchronization: Short-held std::sync::Mutex guards; values cloned/Arc-shared after lookup
state.risk: Manual invalidation and inconsistent path normalization can create stale or duplicate entries.

state.name: Per-repository write locks
fields: one mutex per normalized repository root
state.synchronization: Mutating operations serialize on the same repository; different repositories may proceed concurrently.
state.risk: Long external processes hold the lock and queue every other write for that repository. Lock map entries are never reclaimed.

state.name: Per-repository status single-flight
fields: one status-scan mutex per caller path
state.synchronization: Second caller waits, then rechecks two-second fresh result
state.risk: Raw string keys can miss deduplication for alternate spellings of the same repository path.

state.name: Late-result guards
state.synchronization: Older results are ignored after completion
state.risk: This is supersession, not cancellation; unguarded new workflows can still apply stale data.

state.name: Staging interaction queue
state.synchronization: 300 ms batching, one active flush, commit waits for staging, 15 s UI safety timeout
state.risk: Backend work can continue after the UI safety timeout; checkbox truth is eventually reconciled by status refresh.

state.name: Backend PR request generations
state.synchronization: Mutex-protected counter; checked before expensive gh round
state.risk: Does not terminate gh calls already running and uses non-canonical repository path keys.

executionFlows.name: Open a repository
executionFlows.trigger: User selects or reopens a repository
executionFlows.summary: Fast Git snapshot paints navigation first; a background full status scan then enables mutations.

steps.operation: Increment repository generation and invoke fast load
Deserialize request and await command
Open repository, read refs/commit window/index metadata
Apply result only if generation still matches; render with statusReady=false
Full status scan, single-flight/cache reuse
Apply status and set statusReady=true if repository identity still matches

executionFlows.concurrency: Fast result and later status completion are sequential for one open, while a newer open can supersede their frontend application.
risks: Mutations are deliberately refused until status is known
The scan itself can be expensive on large Windows worktrees

executionFlows.name: Stage and commit selected changes
executionFlows.trigger: Working-tree checkboxes, Stage all or Commit
executionFlows.summary: Frontend batches selection changes; backend partitions parent/submodule paths, serializes mutations and refreshes status.

steps.operation: Optimistically queue checkbox intent for 300 ms
Acquire repository lock and mutate index
Invalidate affected caches
Reconcile visible status
Wait for active staging flight before commit
Acquire write lock, write tree and commit

executionFlows.concurrency: Frontend serializes its staging flight; the backend write lock serializes same-repository mutations. Other repositories can mutate in parallel.
risks: The 15-second frontend flush timeout does not cancel backend work

executionFlows.name: Open a submodule branch map
executionFlows.summary: The selected path is validated against the parent's exact gitlink, then the child repository gets its own isolated graph state.

steps.operation: Capture relative path/name and increment generation
Resolve and open the exact child repository, never discover upward
Build child refs, commits, status and identity
Apply only matching result to isolated submodule graph state
Build child repository lanes

executionFlows.concurrency: A later submodule selection supersedes earlier UI results; the earlier backend scan still runs.
risks: Context safety depends on every graph consumer using activeGraphData rather than parent state

executionFlows.name: Resolve Pull Request status
executionFlows.trigger: An expanded repository or submodule PR panel loads or polls
executionFlows.summary: Git topology establishes the real head repo/branch, then outgoing and incoming PR queries fan out through gh.

steps.operation: Capture repository/branch context and invoke pr_status
Read actual HEAD, upstream and GitHub remote candidates
Run head and incoming-base candidate queries concurrently
Execute gh with explicit repository slug and JSON fields
Ignore stale generation or render PR/auth/provider state

executionFlows.concurrency: Up to the bounded candidate set is queried in actual native-thread/child-process parallelism. Polling occurs only while a panel is expanded.
risks: No cooperative cancellation once gh begins
Auth and provider failures are external-state dependent

executionFlows.name: Compare local with remote
executionFlows.summary: One relative path drives local filesystem entries and corresponding remote tree entries, with submodule-aware redirection.

steps.operation: Set shared relative path and invoke comparison
Resolve remote commit, submodule boundary, local entries and remote tree
Render merged row model if request guard still matches
Read local file and remote blob
Compute/render line alignment with large-input fallback

executionFlows.concurrency: Navigation and preview requests use separate late-result guards; computation is not cancelable.
risks: Quadratic diff work executes in the WebView for inputs below the fallback threshold

executionFlows.name: Run an embedded Terminal command
executionFlows.summary: Command runs in the selected repository/folder under the repository write lock with prompts disabled.

steps.operation: Confirm destructive-looking commands and block other mutations/repository switching
Dispatch entire blocking body to spawn_blocking
Serialize against all other same-repository mutations
Execute cmd.exe or login shell; capture output
Display exit/result and reload after possibly mutating commands

executionFlows.concurrency: Only one console command is admitted by the UI, and the repository lock prevents same-repository mutations. Independent repository work can run in parallel.
risks: A read-only terminal command still holds the write lock
Intentional arbitrary shell capability has a large authority surface

concurrency.summary: The design combines a single WebView event loop, asynchronous Tauri commands, a blocking worker pool, explicit native threads and child processes. Async is used primarily as a transport to blocking workers; real parallelism comes from the worker pool, scoped PR threads and independent child processes.

contexts.name: WebView UI event loop
contexts.work: DOM events, rendering, state mutation, promise continuations, graph and diff computation
contexts.canBlockOn: Large synchronous JavaScript computations or native sync-command round trips

contexts.name: Tauri synchronous command handler
contexts.work: Every registered Rust pub fn command
contexts.canBlockOn: libgit2, filesystem, mutex waits or child processes inside sync commands

contexts.name: Tauri async runtime
contexts.work: Awaits async commands; does not make inner blocking work safe by itself

contexts.name: Blocking worker pool
contexts.work: Full bodies of selected async commands
contexts.canBlockOn: Repository locks, libgit2/filesystem and external process completion

contexts.name: Child processes + waiter threads
contexts.work: git, gh, shells, browser openers, UTRUD
contexts.canBlockOn: Network, credentials, filesystem locks until completion/timeout

synchronization.purpose: Prevent mutation before a trustworthy status snapshot exists
Reject stale results without canceling work

synchronization.scope: One mutex per global cache map

parallelism: Operations against distinct repositories can execute concurrently on blocking workers.
Read operations not using the write lock can overlap writes and external filesystem changes.
PR head/base candidate gh calls execute in actual parallel native threads.
Every child process executes independently of JavaScript; same-repository callers may be serialized before launch.
blocking: Sync Tauri endpoints execute their function bodies inline; heavy examples include publish_branch, restore_remote_file, path_history, compare operations, branch/merge/stash operations and some submodule/status helpers.
Long external processes hold a same-repository write lock for their complete lifetime.
Frontend graph layout and LCS comparison execute synchronously on the UI event loop.
cancellation: No general user-visible cancellation token exists.
Request-generation guards provide result supersession, not work cancellation.
spawn_blocking work continues even if its result becomes irrelevant.
Git/terminal/gh child processes stop on completion or the 600-second timeout; timeout force-kills them.
concurrency.deadlockAssessment: No demonstrated deadlock cycle was found. Parent/submodule code explicitly drops one repository guard before acquiring another in important flows. The safety depends on this convention rather than a typed lock-order abstraction, so future nested changes are a watch area.
raceAssessment: External filesystem/Git changes can occur between a cached read and a later action.
Alternate spellings of the same path can split non-canonical cache/status/PR-generation keys.
Any new frontend async workflow that omits a request guard can apply a late result to the wrong context.
Read operations that do not acquire the write lock can observe intermediate external or application-driven state.
contentionPoints: Full worktree status scans on large Windows repositories
Repository write mutex during long network or terminal commands
Repeated cloning of cached status vectors

extensionPoints.name: Remote hosting provider boundary
extensionPoints.currentSituation: Generic Git remote transport and GitHub-specific PR semantics coexist in repository.rs.
extensionPoints.futureDirection: Introduce a small provider capability interface (identity, PR status, build/check status, URLs) behind the existing Tauri DTOs before adding another provider.
extensionPoints.safestIncrement: Extract pure remote parsing/query-plan functions first; preserve command names and result shapes.

extensionPoints.name: Compare → Workbench boundary
extensionPoints.currentSituation: Backend compare helpers are cohesive, but frontend behavior/state live in app.js and assume one synchronized path.
extensionPoints.futureDirection: Define pane locations and source adapters: LocalPathSource, GitTreeSource, later LocalPathSource on both sides. Keep operations behind a Workbench service/controller boundary.
extensionPoints.safestIncrement: First extract current behavior unchanged into a pure row-model plus controller/service facade; add no new mode until regression tests cover current Local↔Origin.

extensionPoints.name: Engineering integration boundary
extensionPoints.currentSituation: Polarion and UTRUD assumptions are embedded in generic frontend/backend modules.
extensionPoints.futureDirection: Configuration-backed capability adapters with explicit platform/host predicates.
extensionPoints.safestIncrement: Move only constants and URL/command builders behind an adapter module while preserving exact outputs.

extensionPoints.name: Typed IPC client boundary
extensionPoints.currentSituation: Command names, mutation classification and argument/result assumptions are duplicated by convention.
extensionPoints.futureDirection: Generate or hand-maintain one small typed JavaScript facade grouped by capability.
extensionPoints.safestIncrement: Wrap existing invoke calls without changing Rust commands or serialized DTOs.

findings.title: Pure graph model is a strong boundary
findings.currentSituation: DAG/reachability/ref selection is isolated from DOM and IPC.
findings.whyItMatters: Graph correctness can evolve with fast deterministic tests.
findings.suggestedDirection: Keep it pure; extend its input/output model rather than importing UI state.
findings.safestIncrement: Add focused cases for every newly discovered graph topology.

findings.title: Fast-first repository open has the right responsiveness shape
findings.currentSituation: Initial metadata renders before the full status scan, while mutations are gated.
findings.whyItMatters: Large worktrees remain navigable without accepting unsafe mutations on unknown state.
findings.suggestedDirection: Preserve the two-phase contract and make it an explicit repository-session service later.
findings.safestIncrement: Characterize timing and state transitions with integration tests before extraction.

findings.title: Exact submodule repository opening protects context correctness
findings.currentSituation: Submodule operations use Repository::open at the known child path and reject missing metadata instead of discovering upward.
findings.whyItMatters: Prevents parent repository history or mutations from being mislabeled as a submodule operation.
findings.suggestedDirection: Keep this invariant in any future repository-context abstraction.
findings.safestIncrement: Preserve and expand exact-root regression tests.

findings.title: Two monolithic orchestrators dominate the architecture
findings.currentSituation: app.js owns presentation, state and workflows; repository.rs owns nearly every backend role.
findings.whyItMatters: Unrelated feature changes share state, review surface and failure blast radius.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: Feature velocity increasingly raises regression and comprehension costs.
findings.suggestedDirection: Incrementally extract vertical capability modules behind current command/result contracts; do not rewrite.
findings.safestIncrement: Start with pure helpers/adapters (provider parsing or Compare row model), add characterization tests, then move code without behavior changes.

findings.title: Costly work remains behind synchronous Tauri commands
findings.currentSituation: Only selected async commands call off_main_thread; many filesystem/libgit2/network/mutation endpoints are synchronous.
findings.whyItMatters: Inline blocking work can delay IPC/event handling and present as an unresponsive window, especially on large Windows repositories.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: Intermittent UI freezes and inconsistent responsiveness remain likely.
findings.suggestedDirection: Classify commands by cost and mutation semantics; route every potentially slow body through one background execution policy while preserving serialization locks.
findings.safestIncrement: Convert one measured slow command at a time to async + off_main_thread with unchanged inner function and DTO, then test ordering/error behavior.

findings.title: Repository and submodule context is implicit in global frontend state
findings.currentSituation: Parent fields and submoduleGraph coexist in one state object; consumers must remember activeGraphData and request guards.
findings.whyItMatters: A missed accessor or identity check can show or operate on the wrong repository.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: Context-related regressions recur as features are added.
findings.suggestedDirection: Introduce immutable RepositoryContext identifiers and pass context into graph/PR/action controllers.
findings.safestIncrement: Add a read-only context object and assertions first; retain existing state fields until every consumer migrates.

findings.title: Shared caches do not use one canonical repository identity
findings.currentSituation: Write locks canonicalize paths, while several caches, scan locks and PR generations use caller strings.
findings.whyItMatters: Case, separators, symlinks or subfolder-discovered paths can split cache entries and single-flight protection.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: Duplicate work and stale/inconsistent state on path-variant platforms, especially Windows.
findings.suggestedDirection: Resolve one RepositoryId at the command boundary and key all per-repository state with it.
findings.safestIncrement: Add a pure canonical-key helper and tests for Windows spelling/case before migrating one cache at a time.

findings.title: Multi-repository lock ordering is convention-based
findings.currentSituation: Submodule workflows deliberately drop child/parent guards before acquiring another lock; no cycle was found.
findings.whyItMatters: Future nested operations could accidentally invert parent/child lock acquisition.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: Currently controlled, but difficult-to-review deadlock risk grows with new workflows.
findings.suggestedDirection: Document and assert a no-nested-repository-lock rule or provide one coordinator for two-repository operations.
findings.safestIncrement: Add lock-order comments/tests and centralized helper APIs without changing operation ordering.

findings.title: Supersession is present, cancellation is not
findings.currentSituation: Frontend generations ignore stale results; spawn_blocking and child processes continue until completion or timeout.
findings.whyItMatters: Obsolete expensive work still consumes threads, processes and repository locks.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: Rapid navigation or repeated actions can waste resources and delay relevant work.
findings.suggestedDirection: Introduce operation IDs and cooperative cancellation only for measured long-running classes; preserve safe cleanup.
findings.safestIncrement: Start with user cancellation for external child processes, where lifecycle is observable, not libgit2 operations.

findings.title: Frontend orchestration has no direct integration test boundary
findings.currentSituation: Graph logic has Node tests and backend has extensive embedded tests, but app.js behavior is exercised manually.
findings.whyItMatters: Async context, status gates, staging queues and dialogs are high-risk paths not covered by deterministic UI tests.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: UI regressions will continue to be found mainly on expensive real repositories/Windows runs.
findings.suggestedDirection: Extract testable frontend controllers/state reducers and add a tiny mocked-invoke browser harness.
findings.safestIncrement: Characterize repository-open generation, submodule context and stage/commit queue before moving implementation.

findings.title: Provider and company-specific integration boundaries are implicit
findings.currentSituation: GitHub, Polarion and UTRUD code sits inside generic controller/repository modules.
findings.whyItMatters: Adding build status, another host or engineering tool expands already-central modules and embeds organizational policy in the core.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: Provider-specific conditionals and configuration assumptions spread across UI and backend.
findings.suggestedDirection: Use capability-oriented provider/adaptor modules with generic DTOs at the application boundary.
findings.safestIncrement: Extract pure parsers/builders first and keep all existing command names and UI behavior.

findings.title: Some registered commands have no direct current frontend invoke site
findings.currentSituation: create_commit, delete_local_path, pop_stash, conflict_sides and run_git_command are registered but no literal invoke call is present in current app.js.
findings.whyItMatters: Legacy surface expands audit and compatibility burden; dynamic or future use remains possible.
findings.suggestedDirection: Confirm with runtime telemetry/tests before deprecating; do not remove speculatively.
findings.safestIncrement: Mark deprecated internally and verify packaged clients before any removal.

findings.title: Compare is cohesive in concept but not yet safe as an independent Workbench
findings.currentSituation: Backend compare helpers form a cluster; frontend state/navigation/diff/restore remain mixed into app.js and assume Local↔Origin synchronized navigation.
findings.whyItMatters: Adding independent Local↔Local panes directly to current globals would multiply navigation and mutation coupling.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: Workbench growth destabilizes repository navigation and recovery workflows.
findings.suggestedDirection: Model two explicit PaneLocation values, pluggable content sources and operations; linked navigation becomes an option rather than an invariant.
findings.safestIncrement: First extract current Local↔Origin row construction and navigation into a tested module with exactly one shared path; introduce independent panes only afterward.

findings.title: Windows executable synchronization is a delivery-state concern
findings.currentSituation: Source and a bundled Windows executable are versioned, while build SHA identifies the source used by a binary.
findings.whyItMatters: A correct source change is not available to Windows users until the artifact is rebuilt and copied/published.
findings.riskIfUnchanged: Testing may unknowingly use an older binary.
findings.suggestedDirection: Treat build identity as the authority and make artifact freshness visible in release checks.
findings.safestIncrement: Add a non-mutating verification step comparing embedded SHA with expected source commit.

uncertainties.statement: Exact OS thread affinity of each Tauri sync IPC callback can vary with runtime/platform implementation.
uncertainties.known: The generated synchronous wrapper calls the Rust body inline and performs no explicit background dispatch.
uncertainties.impact: The safe architectural conclusion is to avoid potentially blocking work in sync handlers; precise thread naming is not required.

uncertainties.statement: Commands with no literal app.js invoke may still be used by older packaged clients, tests or future dynamic callers.
uncertainties.known: They are registered at the analyzed commit and lack a direct literal current-UI invocation.
uncertainties.impact: They are candidates for validation, not proven dead code.

uncertainties.statement: Static analysis identifies blocking and contention mechanisms but cannot assign production latency to each path.
uncertainties.known: The code logs durations and contains caches motivated by measured large-repository costs.
uncertainties.impact: Prioritize conversions using real perf logs rather than line count alone.

architectureStory: GitDrillDown is a desktop Git client whose interface runs as ordinary HTML, CSS and JavaScript inside a Tauri WebView.
When the interface needs repository information or requests a change, it invokes a named Tauri command with the exact repository and path context.
Rust validates that context, coordinates caches and write locks, then uses libgit2, the filesystem or a carefully bounded external process.
The result crosses the same boundary back to JavaScript, where stale-request guards prevent an older response from replacing the screen for a newer context.
